newsitem.title: UK: UK govt deficit headed for undershoot -analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK govt deficit headed for undershoot -analysts.

text.p: Britain's Public Sector Borrowing Requirement (PSBR) should remain safely on course to undershoot the government's annual deficit forecast after February data are released on Tuesday, analysts said on Monday.

Weaker Value Added Tax (VAT) receipts will weigh on the February number with consensus estimates of a 3.7 billion sterling deficit for the month -- a sharp turnaround from the 5.8 billion surplus in January.

"I'm a bit cautious on the tax receipt side because we had such a fantastic figure in January," said Jonathon Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets. "Erratic swings in VAT are the main reasons for the weakness, but that's nothing to worry about."
The market estimates for February translate into a cumulative 11-month deficit of around 14 billion sterling.
The UK Treasury has forecast a 26.5 billion sterling shortfall for the 12 months ending March 1997.
"The deficit looks like it is undershooting by several billion and that is a fairly healthy outcome," said Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers.

"That would be a sign that the government is being very cautious on the spending side when they could have easily tried to cook the books. With the government well behind (in the polls) that is quite an unusual outcome."
But Loynes said that the PSBR was still "coming down rather disappointingly slowly" because the Treasury's 26.5 billion sterling forecast was double its forecast two years ago.
"For that reason I still think there is a good case for a fiscal tightening under the next government," Loynes said.
The biggest wildcard in the figure was the impact of income tax self-assessment for the self-employed, analysts said.
"That is a little bit of an unknown and could result in a bit of a better figure," Loynes said.
